questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: For me personally, it was crucial to study in a German-speaking country, since I am studying German Language and Culture. Having already lived in Berlin during my gap year, and always wanting to return in an academic context, it felt like the natural choice. I was already somewhat familiar with the city, but I also felt there was so much more to explore – especially as a student.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found it very straightforward to access the necessary information after my arrival. Freie Universität (FU) was excellent at continuously sending out all the relevant information before, during, and after arrival via email.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The student information office helped me with guidance on how to obtain a German health insurance, which was necessary in order to be enrolled at the university. Afterwards, they also guided me through the course registration process and explained what I needed to pay attention to.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used the German portal WG-Gesucht to find accommodation. I contacted around 10 different people, and eventually it worked out. If you start looking early and make an effort to reach out to many listings, I definitely think it is possible to find a place to live – though it may be more expensive than living in a student dormitory.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Be aware that commuting times to Freie Universität can be long. I brought my bike and cycled to the university, and I personally enjoyed coming home to a completely different neighborhood than where the university is located. But of course, this is a matter of personal preference.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process at FU was well supported by both UCPH and Freie Universität. The only obstacle I encountered was finding a German insurance provider that could officially confirm to the university that I was properly insured as an EU citizen via the European Health Insurance Card. Eventually, however, I managed to solve this.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The student information office, or the “incoming team” at FU, suggested German insurance companies I could contact. When these companies did not respond, FU encouraged me to visit one in person in Berlin. Once I did so, they immediately helped me sort out the missing document I needed.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very! I was able to register for all the courses I wanted to take – even courses outside of my host department (the Institute for German and Dutch Philology).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure you sort out the documentation for your health insurance. Even if you are covered by the European Health Insurance Card, you will need a German insurance provider to confirm this to FU before you can complete your enrolment.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I have listed the courses I took below, along with the examination formats and how demanding I found them. Overall, I felt that courses designed specifically for exchange students were less demanding than those designed for German students. This was not only due to the language, but also because I chose courses in institutes and subject areas that I had not studied before. Nevertheless, I strongly recommend taking at least one course in German within a subject that you are genuinely interested in, since in my experience the teaching quality at FU was extremely high and enriching.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There were generally three types of teaching at FU: lectures, seminars, and classroom teaching. From my bachelor studies at UCPH, I am most familiar with seminars, where the weekly readings are discussed collectively, or classroom teaching, where new academic topics are introduced and worked with. These two forms at FU were very similar to my German courses at UCPH. Lectures resembled the fællesforelæsninger at UCPH. Overall, I found the courses to be of very high quality, sometimes demanding to keep up with, but the lecturers were generally very helpful and eager to answer any questions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Einführung in die EU (7 ECTS): Written exam in German without aids (with the option to write in English). Weekly lecture (2 hours). Large syllabus, interesting but demanding. Designed for political science students at the Department of Political Science. Attendance fulfilled by giving a presentation.
Deutschlands politische Landschaft: Institutionen und Prozesse (5 ECTS): Written exam in German, handwritten, without aids. Weekly lecture (2 hours). Minimal syllabus, introductory and very manageable. Weekly attendance required, plus a mandatory presentation. Designed for exchange students.
Green Germany (5 ECTS): Written exam in English without aids. Weekly seminar (2 hours), group work and text discussions. With prior knowledge of German history and culture, the workload was moderate. Weekly attendance required. Designed for exchange students.
Hannah Arendt, Vita Activa (5 ECTS): Exam: Hausarbeit (approx. 10 pages in German). We read Hannah Arendt’s Vita Activa in its entirety in German, discussing each chapter in the weekly seminar (2 hours). Exciting, highly educational, but very demanding – both to read the book within the semester and to write the exam paper. Passing required writing at least 6 discussion papers on chapters of choice and moderating one seminar in a group. Designed for German philosophy students.
Language Course: Vertiefungsmodul A (5 ECTS): Weekly language course (4 hours) with both international and German students. Covered grammar and exercises. C1 level, very demanding. Passing required 4 written assignments (with resubmission if necessary) and full attendance. Although the assignments were tough, the feedback was excellent and the course structure well thought out.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: As mentioned, I would recommend German students to take at least one course in German on a topic they find interesting, even if it’s outside their field or seems challenging. Personally, I took the course on Hannah Arendt, a thinker I only knew by name beforehand, and although it was by far the most demanding course (in philosophy, very different from German studies), I learned a great deal both academically and personally.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Before departure, I was not aware that one has to pay a license fee, or “Rundfunkbeitrag,” when living in an apartment in Germany. After registering at the Bürgeramt, I received a letter requiring me to pay the fee, which amounted to around 1,500 DKK for 7 months.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Living expenses, especially food and drinks, were cheaper than expected. Additionally, after paying the semester contribution, students receive the “Deutschlandticket,” which grants unlimited travel on all public transportation in Germany (except high-speed trains). I found this a fantastic benefit.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were countless opportunities for students at FU. I mainly explored the sports activities, where a catalogue offered everything from dance, yoga, pilates, kickboxing, and tennis, to much more. Many of these activities were advertised around campus, making it easy to find something that matched your interests.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I found it very rewarding to take part in an activity like tennis or yoga. Beyond that, I recommend exploring the city itself: discover the places you like, set aside time for adventures, and keep at least one day a week free from studies to enjoy Berlin. Use that time either individually or with others to experience the city.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Take a day trip to Potsdam to visit Sanssouci Palace. In summer or on warm days, Berlin’s nearby lakes are perfect for swimming – I especially liked Schlachtensee, Teufelsee, Krummelanke, and Flughafensee. Leipzig is also a great weekend destination, especially during their book fair. From Berlin, it is easy to reach many major European cities, so I highly recommend traveling if you enjoy it. Personally, however, I found Berlin itself so vast and diverse that there was always more to discover within the city.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: As a German student who had previously lived in Berlin, it felt very natural for me to adjust. For those unfamiliar with Berlin, the city can feel overwhelming at first, but once you establish your own daily rhythm, meet people, and find your favorite spots, the city opens up in a very unique way that I haven’t experienced elsewhere.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Take courses in German, join study groups, and get involved. For me, my first contact with local students was purely academic, but gradually this developed into friendships outside the classroom. It may feel intimidating at first, but it pays off. I also signed up for a tandem partner program at FU, where I was paired with a German student who wanted to learn Danish. This was another excellent way to meet local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In professional and academic settings in Germany, professors, lecturers, and staff are still addressed very formally. I didn’t find this a problem, but it does require a shift in mindset compared to Denmark. Despite the formal tone, I always felt that both lecturers and fellow students were approachable, helpful, and eager to support me.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The inclusivity. Both Berlin as a city and FU as a university embrace diversity and are welcoming to everyone, which I greatly appreciated.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
First and foremost, I would encourage everyone to ask for help with the things that may seem incomprehensible or overwhelming, whether practical or academic matters. I had an incredible number of questions and at times along the way I doubted whether I would manage to sort everything out, but it really helped to reach out again and again – and it will work out, as long as you ask when in doubt.

In the academic context, I would like to point out that you may take on a different role or study experience than the one you are used to back home. However, you should not let this intimidate you, but instead take it as part of the experience and accept that it is okay to be more quiet, reserved, etc. – but on the other hand also dare to speak up or throw yourself into something when you feel you have something to contribute.

For the third point, I would simply encourage other students to immerse themselves in experiencing Berlin as a city and to make use of the many opportunities it has to offer for every taste. In doing so, you can gain a special personal connection to the city, and I believe this makes it a place you will want to return to in the future.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Through the introductory language course (Vorkurs), I had the opportunity to apply for a mentor and was paired with a local student studying German literature. We met weekly to discuss assignments, questions, and all sorts of topics. This was an extremely valuable and positive experience, which I would highly recommend to others.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Realizing how much I am capable of when I challenge myself academically. In addition, forming friendships with students from Berlin and from all over the world has been an incredible experience, and I look forward to keeping in touch with them in the future.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Taking courses in German at the same level as local students. It was extremely demanding, but I managed to succeed, and I am very proud of that.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
